description: We’re a team of Computer Science students taking on Dancing with the SARs! We’re interested in AI, ML, data science, and software development, and excited to explore how NASA’s NISAR data can help detect changes on Earth’s surface. We’re looking for creative, motivated teammates with skills in Python, AI/ML,remote sensing, data analysis, visualization, or web development. Curiosity, teamwork, and a willingness to learn are always welcome! 🚀
summary:
SAR Detective is an interactive web app that makes radar satellite imagery understandable to anyone, not just remote-sensing experts. Radar can see Earth's surface through clouds and darkness, but SAR images are grainy, grayscale and hard to read without training, so most people never use this data.

The app uses radar data from the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission (GCOV products from NASA Earthdata), with NASA Worldview/GIBS imagery for context. Users explore an interactive map and compare optical and radar views side by side. They can highlight surface types such as water, vegetation and urban areas. A lightweight machine-learning model classifies radar patterns, and an AI assistant explains in plain language what the user is seeing, for example why a river looks dark or why cities look bright.

This matters because radar watches our planet constantly, through floods, storms and nights. By turning complex SAR observations into something people can explore, SAR Detective can help students, journalists and local communities understand how Earth is changing.
details: SAR Detective is a website that shows where the ground changed after a flood, using NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar, which sees through storm clouds that block ordinary satellite photos. We tested it on the October 2026 San Juan River flood in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, comparing two NISAR GCOV scenes taken 12 days apart on the same track (Oct 14 and Oct 26). In a reproducible Colab notebook, we applied the product's quality masks, filtered radar speckle, corrected a −0.57 dB processing offset, and flagged pixels whose radar echo changed by 3 dB or more. Flagged change was about 8× more common within 200 m of the river than 1 km or more away (2.85% vs 0.35%), and the USGS river gauge independently confirms the flood timing. The live site has a before/after slider, a change map with the river overlay, example spots, a printable report, an open API, and a question box that answers only from our verified results. It's meant to help residents, responders and planners see where to look after a flood without needing radar expertise, while being honest about limits, such as not being able to confirm whether a specific street flooded. What makes it creative is its built-in near-river vs. far-from-river control, a deliberately shown false-alarm spot, and the grounded question box, instead of just a raw radar image. We based our choices on using a real, verifiable event, the timing of the passes, data quality and processing differences, the change threshold, a non-expert audience, and reproducibility. We built it with Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Google Colab, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj, pandas, Matplotlib, earthaccess, FastAPI, Leaflet, Vercel and GitHub, with Claude (Anthropic) used for coding assistance and grounded answers.
